newsitem.title: FRANCE: French teachers go on strike to protest job cuts.
newsitem.headline: French teachers go on strike to protest job cuts.

text.p: French teachers unions are predicting a huge turnout for Monday's teachers' strike, which is expected to close down most French schools in a protest over government plans to eliminate some 2,300 education jobs.
Organisers say protests are scheduled in each of France's 96 departments and add that administrative personnel will join teachers in keeping away from the schools during the one-day action.
The government has announced plans to eliminate more than 5,000 jobs in primary and secondary education in 1997 while creating 2,700 posts in higher education.
That will mean, on balance, 2,300 fewer jobs.
"We are sacrificing the future of education. Education is no longer a national priority," said Guy Le Neouannic of the National Education Federation, one of the sponsoring unions.

The government, under fire for its budget and economic policies after unemployment reached a record 12.6 percent last month, will be closely watching the teachers as a measure of national dissatisfaction with the programme of Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
Labour leaders have been predicting significant unrest in the coming months, and a massive civil service strike has been set for October 17.

Public opinion polls show Juppe's popularity ratings at near-record lows, and some deputies in the governing centre-right have begun openly pleading for a change in priorities well ahead of 1998 general elections.

But so far there has been little evidence of dissatisfaction of the magnitude that led to last year's crippling public-sector strikes, which virtually paralysed France for a four-week period during November and December.
However, major railway unions last week called on their members to join civil service unions in an October 17 national strike.
The civil service workers want talks on pay raises and a reversal of government plans to cut 6,000 jobs next year.
The rail workers want assurances the government will not soon try to privatise the national rail system or cut payrolls.
Monday's teachers strike was set on September 3 by five trade unions representing some 825,000 teachers.
